# Politics

Aristotle. *Politics*. Translated by Benjamin Jowett. [Internet Classics Archive witness](https://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/politics.1.one.html). Selected sections read on 8 September 2026: I.3, I.8–10. The host identifies the translator; this receipt does not identify or collate a specific printed edition, Greek text or full work.

The selected account **sources** [the historical branch](../../../../etymologies/apportionment-and-economy/HISTORICAL-BRANCHES.md) and **qualifies** its [whole-field](../../../../etymologies/apportionment-and-economy/WHOLE-FIELD.md). The historical proposition and Taylor’s relational operation retain distinct authority.

## Selected passages

<a id="aristotle-politics-jowett-q001"></a>
### q001 — The household’s distinct relations

**Paraphrase:** The account identifies master and enslaved person, husband and wife, and parent and child as household relations. Acquisition is a further disputed component. This setting is retained in the later account of provision and cannot be silently converted into a modern association of equal governors.

**Locator:** I.3.

**Verification:** selected Benjamin Jowett online translation read; paraphrase-ready, no print or Greek collation and no exact quotation claim.

<a id="aristotle-politics-jowett-q002"></a>
### q002 — Provision, use and accumulation

**Paraphrase:** Acquisition provides what household management uses. A shoe can serve wear or exchange; coined money facilitates exchange, and accumulation can become a separate unlimited end. Aristotle distinguishes this end from bounded provision and censures usury. These are his evaluative distinctions and origin narrative. The text’s endorsement of hierarchy and coercive acquisition remains part of its historical position.

**Locator:** I.8–10.

**Verification:** selected Benjamin Jowett online translation read; paraphrase-ready, no print or Greek collation and no exact quotation claim.
